--- course-unit: a03-discrete-event-simulation status: complete --- # Discrete-event simulation {#sec-discrete-event-simulation} ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} **Self-study**: not taught at the workshop, but complete and ready to use on your own. ::: The jump-process chapter simulates a continuous-time Markov chain by tracking *aggregate counts* and repeatedly asking "what happens next, and to how many people?" The agent-based model chapter tracks *individuals*, but advances them in fixed time steps of $\Delta t = 0.1$. A discrete-event simulation (DES) combines both ideas: it tracks individuals **and** advances time continuously, jumping directly from one scheduled event to the next without ever discretizing the clock. This appendix builds the same SIR process as an event queue two different ways — with Agents.jl's current `EventQueueABM`, and with the general-purpose process-oriented `ConcurrentSim.jl` — and shows how naturally a DES can express things the earlier chapters could not, including the fixed delay of @sec-delay-differential-equations. ## Learning goals By the end of this unit you should be able to: - classify an individual-level, continuous-time, event-queue simulation and contrast it with the population-level CTMC (jump-process chapter) and the discrete-time ABM (agent-based models chapter); - construct an `EventQueueABM` with `AgentEvent`s whose propensities depend on agent state, using the current Agents.jl 7 API; - construct an equivalent model with `ConcurrentSim.jl`'s coroutine-based processes, and explain when its more general process/resource abstraction is preferable to an agent-centric framework; - validate a DES implementation with conservation, monotonicity of the one-way $S\to I\to R$ transition, and an ensemble comparison against the deterministic mean field; and - recognize how an event's *timing* function, not just its propensity, can encode a fixed delay directly, connecting back to the method of steps. ## Model assumptions and classification The population and rates are the usual baseline: $N=1000$, $S(0)=990$, $I(0)=10$, $R(0)=0$, contact rate $c=10$, transmission probability $\beta = 0.05$, recovery rate $\gamma=0.25$. Each individual is in exactly one of three states. A susceptible individual's next contact, and an infectious individual's recovery, are each scheduled as an **event** at a specific future time; the simulation clock jumps directly to the next scheduled event anywhere in the population, executes it, and reschedules as needed. There is no fixed time step anywhere in the model. | Property | Classification | |---|---| | Determinism | Stochastic | | Time | Continuous, event-driven (no fixed $\Delta t$) | | State | Discrete (individual status) | | Representation | Individual-level | This is a **stochastic, continuous-time, discrete-state, individual-level** model — the same underlying process as the jump-process chapter's CTMC, by the superposition of independent exponential clocks, but resolved per individual rather than by a single aggregate "what happens next" draw, and without the agent-based model chapter's time-step discretization. ## Equations Each susceptible individual's next contact is scheduled after an $\mathrm{Exponential}(1/c)$ waiting time; when that contact fires, a uniformly random other individual is chosen, and infection occurs with probability $\beta$ if the alter is infectious: $$ T_\text{contact} \sim \mathrm{Exponential}(1/c), \qquad \Pr(\text{infect} \mid \text{contact with infectious alter}) = \beta. $$ {#eq-a03-contact} Each infectious individual's recovery fires after an independent $\mathrm{Exponential}(1/\gamma)$ waiting time: $$ T_\text{recovery} \sim \mathrm{Exponential}(1/\gamma). $$ {#eq-a03-recovery} By the memoryless property and superposition of independent Poisson processes, the *population-level* counting process implied by @eq-a03-contact and @eq-a03-recovery is exactly the CTMC of the jump-process chapter; the individual-event view additionally retains *who* infected *whom* and *when* each specific event is scheduled, which an event queue (a priority queue ordered by event time) makes explicit. ## Julia implementation ### Primary: `Agents.jl` `EventQueueABM` `EventQueueABM` associates each agent with one or more `AgentEvent`s. By default `AgentEvent`'s `timing` samples an exponential waiting time parameterized by the event's `propensity`, exactly matching @eq-a03-contact–@eq-a03-recovery; only agents with nonzero propensity are scheduled. ::: {#cell-code-a03-setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Agents using ConcurrentSim using ResumableFunctions using Random using Distributions using DataFrames using OrdinaryDiffEq using CairoMakie const β = 0.05 const c = 10.0 const γ = 0.25 const N = 1000 const I0 = 10 const tf = 40.0 ``` ::: {#code-a03-setup .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 40.0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-code-a03-eventqueue .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} @agent struct Person(NoSpaceAgent) status::Symbol end function transmit!(agent, model) alter = random_agent(model) if alter.status == :I && (rand(abmrng(model)) ≤ model.β) agent.status = :I end return nothing end recover!(agent, model) = (agent.status = :R) transmit_propensity(agent, model) = agent.status == :S ? model.c : 0.0 # eq-a03-contact recovery_propensity(agent, model) = agent.status == :I ? model.γ : 0.0 # eq-a03-recovery transmit_event = AgentEvent(action! = transmit!, propensity = transmit_propensity) recovery_event = AgentEvent(action! = recover!, propensity = recovery_propensity) events = (transmit_event, recovery_event) susceptible(x) = count(==(:S), x) infected(x) = count(==(:I), x) recovered(x) = count(==(:R), x) function init_eventqueue_model(β, c, γ, N, I0, rng) properties = Dict(:β => β, :c => c, :γ => γ) model = EventQueueABM(Person, events; properties, rng) for i in 1:N status = i <= I0 ? :I : :S add_agent!(Person(; id = i, status = status), model) end return model end rng = Xoshiro(20250711) eq_model = init_eventqueue_model(β, c, γ, N, I0, rng) to_collect = [(:status, f) for f in (susceptible, infected, recovered)] eq_data, _ = run!(eq_model, tf; adata = to_collect) first(eq_data, 3) ``` ::: {#code-a03-eventqueue .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Alternative: `ConcurrentSim.jl` general-purpose processes `ConcurrentSim.jl` (the maintained continuation of the historical `SimJulia`) is not agent-centric: it provides coroutine-based *processes* that `timeout` for arbitrary durations, plus general `Resource`/`Store` primitives for queueing and contention. Where `EventQueueABM` gives you propensities and actions, `ConcurrentSim` gives you the process itself as a Julia function — more bookkeeping, but no requirement that the model be phrased as "agents with events." Each individual here is a `@resumable` process that repeats "wait for a contact, maybe get infected" until infected, then waits once more to recover. ::: {#cell-code-a03-concurrentsim .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} mutable struct SIRPerson id::Int status::Symbol end mutable struct SIRModel sim::Simulation β::Float64 c::Float64 γ::Float64 ta::Vector{Float64} Sa::Vector{Int} Ia::Vector{Int} Ra::Vector{Int} people::Vector{SIRPerson} end function record!(m::SIRModel) push!(m.ta, now(m.sim)) push!(m.Sa, count(p -> p.status == :S, m.people)) push!(m.Ia, count(p -> p.status == :I, m.people)) push!(m.Ra, count(p -> p.status == :R, m.people)) return nothing end @resumable function live(sim::Simulation, person::SIRPerson, m::SIRModel, rng) while person.status == :S @yield timeout(sim, rand(rng, Exponential(1 / m.c))) # eq-a03-contact alter = person while alter === person alter = rand(rng, m.people) end if alter.status == :I && rand(rng) < m.β person.status = :I record!(m) end end if person.status == :I @yield timeout(sim, rand(rng, Exponential(1 / m.γ))) # eq-a03-recovery person.status = :R record!(m) end end function init_concurrentsim_model(S, I, R, β, c, γ) sim = Simulation() people = SIRPerson[] for i in 1:S push!(people, SIRPerson(i, :S)) end for i in 1:I push!(people, SIRPerson(S + i, :I)) end for i in 1:R push!(people, SIRPerson(S + I + i, :R)) end SIRModel(sim, β, c, γ, [0.0], [S], [I], [R], people) end cs_rng = Xoshiro(20250711) cs_model = init_concurrentsim_model(N - I0, I0, 0, β, c, γ) for person in cs_model.people @process live(cs_model.sim, person, cs_model, cs_rng) end run(cs_model.sim, tf) (cs_model.Sa[end], cs_model.Ia[end], cs_model.Ra[end]) ``` ::: {#code-a03-concurrentsim .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (147, 7, 846) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-a03-trajectories .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t) S, I, R = u β, c, γ = p Ntot = S + I + R λ = β * c * I / Ntot du[1] = -λ * S du[2] = λ * S - γ * I du[3] = γ * I return nothing end sol_ode = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], (0.0, tf), (β, c, γ)), Tsit5()) fig = Figure(size = (720, 440)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time", ylabel = "infectious count", title = "Two discrete-event realizations vs the ODE mean field") stairs!(ax, eq_data.time, eq_data.infected_status; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 2, label = "I (EventQueueABM)") stairs!(ax, cs_model.ta, cs_model.Ia; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 2, label = "I (ConcurrentSim)") lines!(ax, sol_ode.t, sol_ode[2, :]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 2, label = "I (ODE mean field)") axislegend(ax; position = :rt) fig ``` ::: {#fig-a03-trajectories .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Two independent discrete-event realizations of the same SIR process — Agents.jl's EventQueueABM and ConcurrentSim's process model — against the deterministic ODE mean field. The EventQueueABM curve is coarser because its adata collection samples the model once per unit time by default, while ConcurrentSim's manual bookkeeping records every individual event. ::: ::: ## Validation **Conservation.** Every recorded row of both simulations must sum to $N$: ::: {#cell-code-a03-check-conservation .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} conserved_eq = all(r -> r.susceptible_status + r.infected_status + r.recovered_status == N, eachrow(eq_data)) conserved_cs = all(cs_model.Sa .+ cs_model.Ia .+ cs_model.Ra .== N) (conserved_eq, conserved_cs) ``` ::: {#code-a03-check-conservation .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (true, true) ``` ::: ::: **Monotonicity.** Because transitions are strictly $S \to I \to R$, the susceptible count can only fall and the recovered count can only rise: ::: {#cell-code-a03-check-monotone .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} mono_eq = issorted(eq_data.susceptible_status; rev = true) && issorted(eq_data.recovered_status) mono_cs = issorted(cs_model.Sa; rev = true) && issorted(cs_model.Ra) (mono_eq, mono_cs) ``` ::: {#code-a03-check-monotone .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (true, true) ``` ::: ::: **Ensemble comparison with the mean field.** A small ensemble of `EventQueueABM` runs should scatter around the deterministic prediction: ::: {#cell-code-a03-check-ensemble .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} finals = Int[] for seed in 1:20 ensemble_rng = Xoshiro(seed) ensemble_model = init_eventqueue_model(β, c, γ, N, I0, ensemble_rng) ensemble_data, _ = run!(ensemble_model, tf; adata = to_collect) push!(finals, last(ensemble_data).recovered_status) end mean_final_R = sum(finals) / length(finals) ode_final_R = sol_ode.u[end][3] (mean_final_R, round(ode_final_R; digits = 1), abs(mean_final_R - ode_final_R) / ode_final_R < 0.1) ``` ::: {#code-a03-check-ensemble .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (771.4, 775.7, true) ``` ::: ::: All checks pass: both implementations conserve $N$ exactly, both respect the one-way state ordering, and the 20-run ensemble mean final size is within 10% of the deterministic prediction — consistent given the ensemble is small and some realizations have not fully burned out by $t=40$. ## Interpretation and limitations Both implementations encode identical dynamics, but the two frameworks make different things easy. `EventQueueABM` handles scheduling and bookkeeping automatically once propensities are declared, and its `adata` mechanism is convenient — but by default it samples the model once per unit time, coarser than the true event resolution, as the visibly "steppier" red curve in @fig-a03-trajectories shows. `ConcurrentSim` requires writing the recording logic by hand, but every event is available exactly when it happens, and its general `Resource`/`Store` primitives (queues, limited capacity, priorities) extend naturally to models that are not naturally agent-centric — a patient-flow model with a limited number of hospital beds, for instance, maps directly onto a `ConcurrentSim` `Resource` but has no obvious `EventQueueABM` analogue. Both frameworks share a structural limitation relative to the aggregated jump-process chapter: scheduling and executing $O(N)$ individual events is more expensive than resampling a single aggregate "what happens next," so neither scales as well to very large populations. The specific transmission rule used here — every susceptible polls a uniformly random alter — is also deliberately inefficient (it costs one event per susceptible regardless of how few individuals are infectious), matching the reference tutorials this appendix is based on; a production-oriented implementation would instead schedule new infection attempts only from currently infectious individuals. Finally, notice that nothing here required an exponential recovery time. `AgentEvent`'s `timing` argument accepts any function `timing(agent, model, propensity)`, not just the default exponential sampler, and `ConcurrentSim`'s `timeout` accepts any waiting time, fixed or random. A discrete-event framework can therefore encode the *exact* fixed recovery delay of @sec-delay-differential-equations directly — Exercise 1 asks you to do exactly that — without any history function or method of steps, because the individual retains its own infection time rather than solving a continuous population-level state. For the current APIs, see the [Agents.jl EventQueueABM documentation](https://juliadynamics.github.io/Agents.jl/stable/api/#Agents.EventQueueABM) and the [ConcurrentSim.jl repository](https://github.com/JuliaDynamics/ConcurrentSim.jl). Agents.jl itself is described in [@datseris2022]. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#a03-ex1} Modify the `EventQueueABM` recovery event so that its `timing` function returns a fixed value $\tau = 1/\gamma = 4$ instead of sampling an exponential distribution — keep `recovery_propensity` constant and nonzero for infectious agents, and write `fixed_delay_timing(agent, model, propensity) = agent.status == :I ? τ : Inf` as the event's `timing`. Run the modified model and compare its infectious curve with the deterministic DDE of @sec-delay-differential-equations at the same parameters. Explain why this individual-level construction reaches the same fixed-delay assumption without a history function. ### Exercise 2 {#a03-ex2} Extend the `ConcurrentSim` model with a `Resource` representing a limited number of hospital beds: an infectious individual must successfully `request` a bed before starting the recovery `timeout`, and must `release` it on recovery. Run the model with a small number of beds (for example, 50) and compare the infectious curve and the time individuals spend waiting for a bed with the unconstrained model above. Explain why this kind of resource contention has no natural equivalent in the `EventQueueABM` formulation used in this appendix. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/appendices/03-discrete-event-simulation.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/appendices/03-discrete-event-simulation.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/appendices/03-discrete-event-simulation.jl)
